channel.title: RetroClips — New Films
channel.description: New public-domain film clips added to RetroClips.

item.title: Tumbleweeds (1925)
item.description: The Cherokee Strip land rush — Tumbleweeds restages the actual 1893 Cherokee Strip land rush with a cast of hundreds, and it was William S. Hart's final film after a career as one of the silent Western's biggest stars. A 1939 re-release added an eight-minute spoken prologue, the only time Hart's voice was ever captured on film, reflecting on what he called "the glories of the old west." The site's other Westerns cover the wagon trail (The Covered Wagon) and the railroad (The Iron Horse); this fills in the land rush.

item.title: The Ocean Waif (1916)
item.description: "Let me see whether you're real flesh" — Alice Guy-Blache directed her first film in 1896 at Gaumont, making her arguably cinema's first-ever narrative filmmaker; by the time she made this film in 1916 she was running her own US studio, Solax. Only about 40 minutes of the original roughly 50-minute release survive, preserved by the Library of Congress with visible nitrate decomposition in places. It's her second film on this site alongside Falling Leaves (1912).

item.title: The Kiss (1896)
item.description: The first kiss ever filmed — At eighteen seconds long, this is essentially cinema's very first kiss and its very first scandal in the same breath. Chicago publisher Herbert S. Stone called it "absolutely disgusting" and demanded police intervention, one of the earliest calls for film censorship in American history. It predates every other film on this site, reenacting the stage finale of the Broadway hit The Widow Jones just one year after commercial film exhibition began.

item.title: The Curse of Quon Gwon (1916)
item.description: Styling a sister's hair — This is considered the earliest surviving Chinese American film and one of the earliest US films directed by a woman. Marion Wong founded the Mandarin Film Company at just 21 years old specifically to counter the "yellow peril" caricatures common in films of the era, casting her own family as the crew and cast. The film was never commercially released, and only two of an estimated seven or eight reels survive, rescued decades later from a relative's garage; it entered the National Film Registry in 2006.

item.title: The Cocoanuts (1929)
item.description: Harpo's wordless solo — The Cocoanuts was the Marx Brothers' first film, adapted from their 1925 Broadway hit with songs by Irving Berlin and a book by George S. Kaufman. Harpo's silent harp solo debuts here and became a signature bit in every subsequent Marx Brothers picture. A persistent piece of trivia credits this film's inventive overhead dance shots to Busby Berkeley, but that's a myth: they're the work of co-director Robert Florey, a full year before Berkeley's own screen debut.

item.title: Shoes (1916)
item.description: A pair she can't afford — Shoes takes its title's central symbol and makes it literal in this one striking visual-effects shot, expressing poverty and desperation without a word of dialogue. Lois Weber adapted it from a Stella Wynne Herron short story with input from social reformer Jane Addams, and by the mid-1910s Weber was reportedly the highest-paid film director in Hollywood, male or female, and the first woman inducted into the Motion Picture Directors Association. It's her second film on the site alongside Suspense (1913).

item.title: Fantasmagorie (1908)
item.description: A bottle becomes an elephant — Fantasmagorie is widely credited as the first fully animated cartoon ever made, extending this site's animation history further back than either Gertie the Dinosaur or The Cameraman's Revenge. Émile Cohl hand-drew roughly 700 images and filmed them in negative so the white chalk-like lines would read against a black background. He went on to make over 250 animated films between 1908 and 1923, though most are now lost.

item.title: El Automóvil Gris (1919)
item.description: Forged papers at the door — El Automóvil Gris dramatizes a real 1915 Mexico City crime spree, in which a gang dressed as officials or soldiers used fake credentials to rob the homes of the city's wealthiest residents during the Revolution; several of the actual detectives who caught them played themselves in the film. Director Enrique Rosas died in 1920, shortly after its original release as a 12-episode serial; the surviving version streaming today is a 1933 sound-era re-edit of the same footage. It's one of the earliest Mexican narrative features to survive at all.

item.title: Assunta Spina (1915)
item.description: Flirting at a garden party — Assunta Spina was shot almost entirely on real Naples streets and markets rather than studio sets, a naturalism its star Francesca Bertini herself called a forerunner of what became Italian neorealism decades later. Bertini was one of silent cinema's first global superstars, and film historians widely consider her an uncredited co-director despite the formal credit going to her co-star Gustavo Serena, a common arrangement for the era's leading "diva" actresses.

item.title: The Toll of the Sea (1922)
item.description: An embrace in the garden — This was only the second Technicolor film ever made and the first Technicolor feature shot in Hollywood, and unlike the earlier The Gulf Between, which survives only in fragments, this one exists complete. It was also Anna May Wong's first leading role, taken at seventeen, on her way to becoming the first Chinese-American star Hollywood ever built around. The two-strip color process could only reproduce reds and greens, which is exactly why this garden setting, all jade robes and red roses, was chosen: it is a film built specifically to show off what the new color technology could do.

item.title: The Ten Commandments (1923)
item.description: Moses parts the Red Sea — This is the silent, biblical-prologue half of DeMille's first Ten Commandments, made three decades before his own more famous 1956 remake with Charlton Heston, and the Red Sea effect here was achieved by combining footage of real waves with a giant tank and traveling matte work that was considered borderline miraculous in 1923. DeMille buried an entire full-scale Egyptian city set, sphinxes and all, in the Guadalupe-Nipomo Dunes in California after filming wrapped rather than pay to haul it out, and archaeologists have spent decades since digging pieces of it back up.

item.title: The Sentimental Bloke (1919)
item.description: The Bonzer Peach — The Sentimental Bloke is routinely cited as the greatest Australian silent film and broke national box-office records at its October 1919 Melbourne Town Hall premiere. It's based on C.J. Dennis's 1915 verse novel The Songs of a Sentimental Bloke, written entirely in broad Australian larrikin slang that the film's intertitles preserve straight from the poem. Co-star Lottie Lyell, who plays the sweetheart Doreen, also co-wrote and edited the film, and is now recognized as one of early Australian cinema's most significant behind-the-camera figures rather than just its leading lady.

item.title: The Perils of Pauline (1914)
item.description: The balloon lifts off — This was the original cliffhanger blockbuster, a serial popular enough that William Randolph Hearst ran a matching newspaper serialization alongside it, an early and deliberate cross-media marketing stunt. Star Pearl White did her own stunts and nearly paid for this one for real: the balloon in this sequence broke loose during filming and carried her across the Hudson River into a storm before it could be brought down. Most of the original negatives were later lost, so what survives today is largely a European re-edit, which makes any clean surviving footage of it a little bit of a rarity in itself.

item.title: The Passion of Joan of Arc (1928)
item.description: Falconetti's face under interrogation — The Passion of Joan of Arc is built almost entirely out of faces in extreme close-up, an approach so radical for 1928 that Carl Dreyer had sets built and then largely refused to show them, trusting Renee Jeanne Falconetti's performance to carry the film alone. She reportedly never acted again after this role, and film historians still debate how much of her visible anguish was performance versus Dreyer's famously punishing directing methods. The film was thought lost for decades until a nearly pristine print turned up in a Norwegian mental institution's closet in 1981.

item.title: The Oyster Princess (1919)
item.description: The newlyweds race down the grand staircase — Lubitsch later pointed to this film as the birth of what critics would call the Lubitsch touch, his knack for turning a sight gag into social satire. He was a German director who had never been to America, yet built this farce entirely around mocking American nouveau-riche excess, with a heroine whose father is introduced as the Cotton King and then, a title card later, corrected to the Potash King. The film's real showpiece is a later ensemble dance number so wild it required its own choreographer, but this staircase run captures the same manic, joyful energy in miniature.

item.title: The Life and Death of 9413, a Hollywood Extra (1928)
item.description: Branded on arrival — This is one of the founding works of American avant-garde cinema, reportedly made for around 97 dollars using cigar boxes, tin cans, and toy trains as miniature studio sets, shot largely by two aspiring filmmakers with borrowed equipment and no major-studio backing. It's widely credited with importing German Expressionist visual technique into American independent film, and co-director Slavko Vorkapich went on to invent the rapid-cut transition sequence that became a Golden Age Hollywood editing staple, still known in the industry as a Vorkapich montage.

item.title: The Immigrant (1917)
item.description: Bracing against the rolling ship — The Immigrant is one of Chaplin's most acclaimed Mutual shorts, added to the National Film Registry in 1998 for its blend of physical comedy and genuine sympathy for the immigrant experience it depicts. The ship-set opening was filmed on a set mechanically rigged to rock back and forth, sending Chaplin, his fellow actors, and their soup sliding in unison, a practical effect that took real engineering to pull off in 1917. It remains one of the clearest early showcases of Chaplin's gift for turning physical discomfort into pure comic rhythm.

item.title: The Flying Ace (1926)
item.description: Up in the goggles and leather — The Flying Ace was made by Norman Studios in Jacksonville, one of the only Black-owned film production companies of the silent era, and it's the studio's only surviving complete feature, added to the National Film Registry in 2021. The best piece of trivia here is the trick behind the trick: despite being marketed as 'the greatest airplane thriller ever filmed,' the production reportedly used almost no real in-flight photography at all, the biplane was bolted to the ground the whole time, tilted and shot against a moving-cloud backdrop with wind machines doing the rest of the work.

item.title: The Fall of the House of Usher (1928)
item.description: Madeline, doubly exposed — A young Luis Bunuel co-wrote this and worked on the production before quitting partway through over a dispute with Epstein about how faithfully to follow Poe. The following year Bunuel made Un Chien Andalou with Salvador Dali instead, a film already sitting elsewhere on this site, which makes this one something like its more patient, more formal older cousin. Epstein shot much of it with a wind machine and multiple exposures decades before that kind of layering had a name, using slow motion and superimposition for mood rather than shock in a way that reads as strikingly modern for 1928.

item.title: The Extra Girl (1923)
item.description: Walking the world's calmest lion — The Extra Girl was Mabel Normand's final feature film and her last picture for producer Mack Sennett, a comedy about the movie industry itself that turns on Sue mistaking a real lion delivered to the studio for an actor in a costume. The joke very nearly stopped being funny during production: when the real lion later got loose on set, a trainer trying to wrangle it accidentally jabbed Normand with a pitchfork. It's a fitting send-off for a star whose career, like so many in silent Hollywood, was defined as much by industry chaos as by what made it onto the screen.

item.title: The Electric Hotel (1908)
item.description: The hair styles itself — Segundo de Chomon is often called the Spanish Melies, and The Electric Hotel is his best-known surviving trick film, built almost entirely from stop-motion effects where luggage packs itself, boots lace themselves, and hair styles itself with no operator ever entering the frame. Working independently of Melies's own studio, Chomon achieved some of the era's most convincing object animation through frame-by-frame pixilation, painstakingly repositioning each item a fraction at a time between exposures. The film's premise, an imaginary hotel where every mundane task happens automatically, reads almost like an accidental prediction of a century of home-automation advertising.

item.title: The Cat and the Canary (1927)
item.description: Down the cobwebbed hallway — Paul Leni was a German Expressionist import, fresh off directing Waxworks in Berlin, and this was his American debut, a film now credited with more or less inventing the old-dark-house genre: heirs gathered for a will reading, a hooded killer, comic relief undercutting the dread. The template got reused constantly afterward, from The Old Dark House in 1932 through the 1939 Bob Hope remake and beyond. Leni died just two years after making this, only four years after arriving in Hollywood, so this stands as one of the clearest surviving records of a genuinely important but tragically short American career.

item.title: The Cameraman's Revenge (1912)
item.description: The cabaret dancer at the Gay Dragonfly — Ladislas Starevich made this entirely with dead insects rigged into articulated stop-motion puppets, reportedly a workaround after his live beetles refused to perform under studio lights. The technique was so far ahead of anything else being attempted with animation that some contemporary audiences assumed the insects had been trained rather than animated frame by frame, and Starevich never fully explained his methods. It stands as one of the earliest and strangest examples of stop-motion character animation, made in Moscow a full generation before King Kong or the Rankin-Bass holiday specials it quietly anticipates.

item.title: Suspense (1913)
item.description: A car races to the rescue — Lois Weber was the highest-paid, most prolific director in Hollywood by the mid-1910s and arguably America's first major filmmaking star behind the camera, yet she's largely been written out of the standard silent-film canon. Suspense is a genuine piece of film-grammar innovation: it uses a triangular split-screen to show three lines of action happening at once, plus an early subjective point-of-view shot from inside a speeding car, techniques that were still considered daring decades later. The whole film runs about ten minutes and was made on what was, even by 1913 standards, a shoestring budget.

item.title: Speedy (1928)
item.description: Babe Ruth rides in Speedy's cab — Speedy was Harold Lloyd's last silent film, shot largely on real New York City streets rather than a studio backlot, giving it an almost documentary quality of 1920s Manhattan that few other films of the era captured. Babe Ruth appears as himself in a genuine cameo, playing along with the joke that his own reckless cab ride to Yankee Stadium is nearly as thrilling as anything he does on the field. The location shoot reportedly drew real crowds who had no idea they were watching a movie being made, some of whom ended up in the finished film.

item.title: Regeneration (1915)
item.description: The getaway cars pull out — Regeneration is widely credited as the first feature-length gangster film, a slum-kid-to-gang-leader story that a 28-year-old Raoul Walsh shot as his solo directorial debut on location in New York's actual Bowery tenements, using real residents as extras instead of a studio backlot. The film's climactic boat fire was directly inspired by the real 1904 General Slocum disaster, in which a burning excursion steamer killed roughly 1,000 people in the East River, one of the deadliest disasters in New York City history before September 11.

item.title: Raja Harishchandra (1913)
item.description: A fountain in the palace garden — Raja Harishchandra is widely considered India's first feature film, and this is a rare surviving fragment of it: the National Film Archive of India holds only pieces of the first and last reels. Director Dadasaheb Phalke could not find a single woman willing to appear on camera, since acting was considered indecent for women in 1913 Bombay, even actresses he approached refused, so he cast a man, Anna Salunke, to play the queen, making Salunke India's first credited screen actress. Phalke's legacy is now honored every year through the Dadasaheb Phalke Award, India's highest award in cinema.

item.title: Piccadilly (1929)
item.description: Shosho's spotlight dance — Piccadilly gave Anna May Wong one of the only true leading roles a major studio handed a Chinese-American actress in this era, casting her as a scullery maid who becomes a nightclub's sensation. The interracial romance at the story's center was genuinely controversial for 1929, and the film is now regarded as a landmark of early Chinese-American screen representation. Cinematographer Werner Brandes shot the nightclub sequences with a level of Art Deco polish that made this one of the most visually celebrated British silents of its decade, restored decades later by the BFI as a landmark of the era.

item.title: Master of the House (1925)
item.description: Ida makes up the linen cupboard — Master of the House is Dreyer at his most disciplined: nearly the entire film unfolds inside one cramped Copenhagen apartment, and he insisted on building it as a real, fully wired flat rather than a set, so his actors could move through it the way people actually move through a home they have lived in for years. The film's real subject is housework itself, filmed with the same patient attention Dreyer would later bring to Falconetti's face in The Passion of Joan of Arc, and it was a massive hit in Denmark precisely because audiences recognized the unglamorous domestic labor nobody else was bothering to point a camera at.

item.title: Manhatta (1921)
item.description: The ferry brings the city home — Manhatta is widely credited as the first American avant-garde film and the direct model for the city symphony genre that followed, its clearest descendant being Dziga Vertov's Man with a Movie Camera, already on this site. It was the only film collaboration between photographer Paul Strand and Precisionist painter Charles Sheeler, and its intertitles are lines lifted straight from Walt Whitman's poem Mannahatta, pairing 1921 New York with 1860s verse about the same city.
